title: Go Modules: The Field Handbook
summary: A dense, page-by-page tour of Go's module system — go.mod and go.sum mechanics, semantic import versioning, the MVS algorithm, replace/exclude/retract directives, workspaces, vendoring, and build tags. Covers internals, day-to-day commands, trade-offs, and the mistakes that break builds.

chapters.title: Why Modules Exist
points: A module is a collection of packages versioned as one unit, rooted at the directory holding go.mod
Before modules: GOPATH forced all code into $GOPATH/src/<import path>, one global version per dependency
GOPATH had no version records — `go get` always fetched master, so builds were not reproducible
dep, glide, godep, govendor were community band-aids; modules (Go 1.11, default in 1.16) replaced them all
Module path = the import prefix for every package in the module, e.g. `github.com/user/repo`
Package import path = module path + subdirectory: module `example.com/m` + dir `util` = `example.com/m/util`
Module path must be resolvable by the go command: a URL for public repos, or a private path covered by GOPRIVATE
`go mod init example.com/m` creates go.mod; init infers the path from VCS remote or vendor config when omitted
Modules are self-contained: code can live anywhere on disk, not just in GOPATH
GOPATH still exists but only holds the module cache ($GOPATH/pkg/mod) and installed binaries ($GOPATH/bin)
GO111MODULE values: `on` (default since 1.16), `off` (legacy GOPATH mode), `auto` (module mode only inside a module tree)
A repo can hold multiple modules (nested go.mod files); the innermost go.mod wins for a given package
Build reproducibility is the core promise: same go.mod + go.sum + Go version = same bits
Modules are the unit of versioning, dependency, and distribution — not the unit of compilation (packages are)

chapters.title: Anatomy of go.mod
points: `module example.com/m` — declares the module path; changing it changes every consumer's import path
`go 1.22` — the language version line; gates language features and toolchain behavior, NOT a minimum runtime
Since Go 1.21 the `go` line is a hard requirement: a newer `go` line makes older toolchains refuse to build
`toolchain go1.22.3` — the toolchain the go command switches to when the local one is older (Go 1.21+)
`require example.com/dep v1.4.2` — a direct or indirect dependency at a minimum version
`// indirect` marks a requirement not imported by this module's own packages
Indirect entries appear when a dependency lacks its own go.mod, or to record a version bumped by MVS
`exclude example.com/dep v1.4.1` — pretend that one version does not exist during selection
`replace old => new` — swap a module's source or version, main-module only
`retract v1.2.0` — the module author's own withdrawal of a published version
Block form groups directives: `require ( ... )` with one module per line
go.mod is line-oriented and machine-edited: `go mod edit -require=`, `-droprequire=`, `-replace=`, `-go=`
Comments after directives survive `go mod tidy`; free-form ordering does not — tidy sorts and regroups
Every `require` line is a MINIMUM, never a pin and never a maximum
go.mod must be committed; it is the source of truth the build reads before touching the network

chapters.title: Versions and Pseudo-Versions
points: Versions follow SemVer: vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, always with a leading `v`
MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = backwards-compatible feature, PATCH = backwards-compatible fix
Prerelease suffix: `v1.2.0-beta.1` sorts BEFORE `v1.2.0` and is never chosen by @latest
Build metadata `+incompatible` marks a v2+ tag from a repo with no go.mod at that major version
Pseudo-version = synthetic version for an untagged commit: `v0.0.0-20230518120500-abcdef123456`
Pseudo-version format: base version, UTC commit timestamp `yyyymmddhhmmss`, 12-char commit hash
Three pseudo-version shapes: no prior tag (`v0.0.0-`), after a prerelease (`v1.2.3-0.2023...`), after a release (`v1.2.4-0.2023...`)
Pseudo-versions sort below the next real tag, so a real release always wins over a commit-of-the-day
`v0.x.y` carries no compatibility promise — the ecosystem treats every v0 minor as potentially breaking
`@latest` = highest release tag, ignoring prereleases and retracted versions
Other query forms: `@v1.4.2`, `@upgrade`, `@patch`, `@none`, `@<branch>`, `@<commit>`, `@master`
`go get example.com/dep@none` removes the requirement entirely
Tags must be pushed to be usable — a local tag is invisible to the proxy and to `go get`
Unstable-looking version, stable rule: version strings are compared field-by-field numerically, not lexically

chapters.title: Semantic Import Versioning
points: The rule: major version 2 and above must appear in the module path — `example.com/m/v2`
The reason: two incompatible majors are two different modules, so both can coexist in one build
Import compatibility rule: if an import path is unchanged, the package must be backwards compatible
v0 and v1 share the bare path — `example.com/m` covers both; no `/v1` suffix exists
Releasing v2: bump the module line to `module example.com/m/v2`, rewrite every internal self-import to `/v2`, tag `v2.0.0`
Two release layouts: major-version branch (tag v2.0.0 on branch), or major subdirectory (`/v2/go.mod`, tag `v2/v2.0.0`)
Subdirectory layout lets one commit hold several majors; branch layout keeps history linear
`+incompatible`: a v2+ tag WITHOUT a go.mod gets `v2.0.0+incompatible` and is treated as pre-modules code
A module cannot have both `v2.0.0` and `v2.0.0+incompatible` semantics — adding go.mod at v2 supersedes the incompatible path
One build may contain `example.com/m v1.5.0` and `example.com/m/v2 v2.1.0` simultaneously — separate packages, separate types
Consequence: a type from v1 is NOT assignable to the same-named type from v2; conversion code is on you
Diamond dependency across majors is legal and common — libraries can migrate independently
Common mistake: tagging v2.0.0 without changing the module path — consumers get `+incompatible` or a `go.mod has post-v1 module path` error
Error to memorize: "module declares its path as X but was required as Y" = path/major mismatch
Gradual migration path: keep v1 alive with fixes, ship v2 as a new module, deprecate v1 with `// Deprecated:` and `retract`

chapters.title: MVS: How Versions Get Picked
points: Minimal Version Selection: the build uses the MINIMUM version that satisfies all requirements, not the maximum
Algorithm: walk the module requirement graph from the main module, collect every required version of each module, keep the highest of those
"Highest of the minimums" — not "highest available", which is what npm/Cargo-style solvers do
MVS is deterministic and needs no solver, no lockfile-driven backtracking, and no SAT search
Adding a new dependency never silently upgrades unrelated modules — versions only move when you move them
Result: builds are stable over time; a new upstream release does not change your build until you ask
Trade-off: you may sit on an old version far longer than intended, missing fixes — upgrading is an explicit chore
Trade-off: no version ranges or constraint expressions, so no "<2.0" caps; conflicts are resolved by upgrading, never downgrading
Module graph pruning (Go 1.17+): for deps whose go.mod says `go 1.17` or later, only their direct deps' go.mod files are loaded
Pruning makes the graph small and the load fast; the price is more `// indirect` lines recorded in your go.mod
`go mod graph` prints the full requirement edge list `from@version to@version`
`go list -m all` prints the selected version of every module in the build list
`go mod why -m example.com/dep` explains the shortest import path that keeps a module in the build
Downgrading with `go get dep@v1.2.0` may force downgrades of modules that required a higher version
Upgrade commands: `go get -u ./...` (minor+patch), `go get -u=patch ./...` (patch only), `go get dep@latest` (one module)

chapters.title: go.sum, Proxy, and Checksum Database
points: go.sum records cryptographic hashes for every module version in the graph — it is NOT a lockfile
Two lines per module: one for the module zip (`h1:...`) and one for its go.mod (`/go.mod h1:...`)
`h1:` is a base64 SHA-256 of a sorted file-hash listing inside the zip
Verification: any downloaded content whose hash differs from go.sum aborts the build with a SECURITY ERROR
"checksum mismatch" means the upstream content changed for a fixed version — investigate, do not blindly delete go.sum
GOPROXY default: `https://proxy.golang.org,direct` — try the proxy, then fall back to the origin VCS
The proxy is an immutable cache: once a version is fetched, deleted upstream tags still resolve
GONOPROXY / GOPRIVATE bypass the proxy for matching path prefixes (comma-separated glob patterns)
GONOSUMDB / GONOSUMCHECK are obsolete names; use GONOSUMDB's successor GONOSUMCHECK→`GONOSUMDB`→ current `GONOSUMDB`/`GOPRIVATE` + `GONOSUMDB` — practically: set `GOPRIVATE` and it sets both
GOSUMDB default `sum.golang.org` is a transparency log; `GOFLAGS=-mod=mod` and `GONOSUMDB` do not disable it — `GONOSUMDB`/`GOPRIVATE` do
`GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly` is the default since 1.16: the build fails instead of editing go.mod for you
Module cache lives at `$GOPATH/pkg/mod`, read-only on disk; `go clean -modcache` wipes it
`GOMODCACHE` relocates the cache; `GOFLAGS`, `GONOSUMDB`, `GOPRIVATE` are all readable via `go env`
`go mod verify` re-hashes everything in the cache against go.sum
`go mod download` pre-populates the cache — the standard CI warm-up step before the build
Always commit go.sum; deleting it and regenerating trusts whatever the network serves today

chapters.title: replace, exclude, retract, and Workspaces
points: `replace example.com/dep => ../local/dep` — point a dependency at a local directory for live editing
`replace example.com/dep => example.com/fork v1.4.2` — swap in a fork by module path and version
`replace example.com/dep v1.4.1 => example.com/dep v1.4.2` — replace one specific version only
replace directives in NON-main modules are ignored; only the main module's replaces apply
Consequence: publishing a library with a local-path replace breaks every consumer — strip it before tagging
A filesystem replace target must contain its own go.mod, and its own requirements still feed MVS
replace does not change the import path in your source — code still imports the original path
`exclude example.com/dep v1.4.1` — skip a known-bad version; MVS picks the next higher one
exclude is also main-module-only and is rarely the right tool — prefer bumping the require line
`retract v1.3.0` / `retract [v1.0.0, v1.2.0]` — the AUTHOR withdraws versions; add a `// reason` comment
Retracted versions stop appearing in `@latest` and `go list -m -versions`, but remain fetchable if pinned
Retraction is published in a NEW higher version's go.mod — you cannot retract without releasing again
Workspaces (Go 1.18+): `go work init ./a ./b` creates go.work listing multiple local modules
go.work is the multi-repo replacement for scattered replace directives — and should be gitignored for personal setups
go.work directives: `use ./dir`, `replace`, `go`; `GOWORK=off` disables workspace mode for one command
Precedence: go.work replace > main go.mod replace > require

chapters.title: Vendoring
points: `go mod vendor` copies every package needed to build and test the main module into `./vendor`
Only packages actually imported are copied — not whole modules, and not tests of dependencies
`vendor/modules.txt` records module paths, versions, `## explicit` markers, and go versions
modules.txt is verified for consistency against go.mod; a stale mismatch fails the build
Auto-detection: if `./vendor/modules.txt` exists and the go line is 1.14+, `-mod=vendor` is the default
In vendor mode the network and the module cache are never touched — no proxy, no go.sum verification
Force either way: `go build -mod=vendor` or `go build -mod=mod`
Pros: hermetic builds, works offline, survives upstream deletion, whole dependency diff is reviewable in PRs
Cons: repo bloat, noisy diffs, must re-run `go mod vendor` after every dependency change, easy to drift
Vendoring is the answer for airgapped builds and vendor-review compliance; a private proxy (Athens, Artifactory) is the modern alternative
`go mod vendor` drops non-Go assets not needed to build, which breaks deps relying on embedded testdata or generated files
Vendored trees do NOT apply replace directives afresh — replaces are resolved at vendor time and baked in
CI check: run `go mod vendor && git diff --exit-code vendor/` to catch out-of-date vendor dirs
Vendor and workspaces interact poorly: `go work vendor` (Go 1.22+) vendors a whole workspace

chapters.title: Build Tags and Conditional Compilation
points: Modern syntax: `//go:build linux && amd64` on its own line, above package, followed by a blank line
Legacy syntax: `// +build linux,amd64` — comma = AND, space = OR, `!` = NOT; Go 1.17+ writes both, 1.18+ needs only the new one
`gofmt` synchronizes the two forms automatically — never hand-edit only one
The constraint must appear before the package clause with nothing but blank lines and other comments between
Filename-based constraints are implicit: `file_linux.go`, `file_amd64.go`, `file_linux_amd64.go`, `file_windows_test.go`
Recognized filename suffixes are GOOS and GOARCH values only — `foo_prod.go` is NOT a constraint
Boolean grammar in the new form: `&&`, `||`, `!`, parentheses — a real expression, unlike the old comma syntax
Custom tags come from `go build -tags=integration,jsoniter` (comma-separated, or space-separated in older Go)
Implicit tags always available: GOOS, GOARCH, `unix` (1.19+), `cgo`, `gc`/`gccgo`, and every `go1.N` up to the current release
`go1.21` style tags are cumulative: a `go1.21` tag is satisfied by Go 1.22, so it means "1.21 or later"
`//go:build ignore` is a convention, not magic — `ignore` is simply a tag nobody sets, so the file is skipped
Classic use: `//go:build ignore` on a `gen.go` run via `go run gen.go` from a `//go:generate` line
Excluded files are invisible to the compiler AND to `go mod tidy`'s import scan — their imports may vanish from go.mod
Fix for that: `go mod tidy` considers all build tags for GOOS/GOARCH but NOT custom tags — keep tools in a `tools.go` with a build tag plus explicit imports
`go list -tags=integration ./...` and `go vet -tags=...` must be given the same tags or they analyze a different program
Common mistake: missing blank line after `//go:build` makes it a doc comment, silently compiling the file everywhere

chapters.title: Workflow, Pitfalls, and Cheat Sheet
points: Daily loop: edit imports, run `go mod tidy`, review the go.mod diff, commit go.mod and go.sum together
`go mod tidy` adds every missing requirement and removes every unused one — it is the only correct way to prune
`go mod tidy -go=1.21` rewrites the go line and re-prunes the graph for that version's rules
`go get` (Go 1.22+) only edits dependencies; use `go install pkg@version` to install binaries
`go install example.com/cmd/tool@latest` builds a tool ignoring the current module's go.mod entirely
Pin build tools by importing them in a `tools.go` guarded with `//go:build tools`, so tidy keeps their versions
CI recipe: `go mod download` then `go build ./...` then `go test ./...` with `-mod=readonly` (the default)
CI guard: `go mod tidy && git diff --exit-code go.mod go.sum` fails the build on an untidy tree
Pitfall: committing a local `replace ... => ../x` — works for you, breaks everyone; use go.work instead
Pitfall: `missing go.sum entry; to add it: go mod download <mod>` — means go.sum is stale, not that the dep is missing
Pitfall: private repos over HTTPS need `GOPRIVATE=github.com/org/*` plus a git credential helper or `insteadOf` SSH rewrite
Pitfall: force-pushing a tag — the proxy already cached the old content, producing a checksum mismatch for everyone
Pitfall: `go get -u ./...` bumps everything at once; prefer targeted upgrades and read release notes
Debugging trio: `go list -m all` (what is selected), `go mod why -m X` (why it is here), `go mod graph` (who required it)
Summary: go.mod = minimums, go.sum = integrity, MVS = highest-of-minimums, /vN = major in path, vendor = hermetic copy, build tags = which files even exist
